video_title: Tracy Britt Cool: The Berkshire Model for $5–50M Businesses
gist: Tracy Britt Cool, Warren Buffett's former chief of staff and ex-CEO of Pampered Chef, explains how Cambrek applies a Berkshire-style long-duration (15+ year), low-leverage, operator-led model to $5-50M-earnings family and founder businesses, sourcing deals through a 4,000-CEO community rather than auctions. She argues multiple arbitrage is over, firms exit compounders too early, and organic operating improvement (35% earnings CAGR, e.g. JM Test 4x) is the return driver.

themes.theme: Berkshire turnaround lessons (Benjamin Moore, Pampered Chef)

insights.claim: Under Berkshire ownership, Benjamin Moore lost its way over a decade: gallon volume fell considerably while earnings stayed flat because management cut marketing spend and took price instead of investing in brand and the dealer channel.
insights.speaker: Tracy Britt Cool
insights.so_what: Flat earnings masking falling unit volume plus shrinking marketing spend is a red flag for brand erosion in branded consumer/building-products businesses.

insights.claim: Tracy Britt Cool's fix at Benjamin Moore as chair was to reinvest in brand, the store experience and the independent dealer channel (rather than pursue big-box partnerships), which significantly improved earnings through volume growth rather than financial engineering.
insights.speaker: Tracy Britt Cool
insights.so_what: Dealer-channel paint brands can recover earnings by reinvesting in the channel; a shift toward big-box was viewed as the wrong strategy for the brand.

insights.claim: Benjamin Moore's decline was rooted in misaligned incentives: management was rewarded for maintaining earnings rather than growing volume and reinvesting in the future of the business.
insights.speaker: Tracy Britt Cool
insights.so_what: When diagnosing an underperforming company, check whether management incentives target near-term earnings preservation over volume/franchise growth.

insights.claim: Looking at a business over a 10-year window reveals declines that yearly reviews explain away as market conditions or anomalies; a 10%+ cumulative volume decline signals a serious problem.
insights.speaker: Tracy Britt Cool
insights.so_what: Use decade-long unit-volume trends, not year-over-year comparisons, to spot slow franchise erosion before it shows up in earnings.
insights.quote: But when you look at 10 over 10 years and your volume's declined, you know, 10 plus percent, then you're like, "Oh wow, there's something serious going on here."

insights.claim: In underperforming companies the solution is usually already known inside the organization; the problem is that leadership isn't getting to it, isn't listening, or other influences are driving wrong decisions.
insights.speaker: Tracy Britt Cool
insights.so_what: Operational due diligence should mine frontline employees and middle management for the turnaround plan rather than importing one.
insights.quote: the reality when doing that is usually the answer is in the building.

insights.claim: Tracy Britt Cool expected the Pampered Chef turnaround (after about a decade of decline) to take 1-2 years but it took nearly 4, because people, culture and retention changes are far harder than investors' spreadsheet assumptions.
insights.speaker: Tracy Britt Cool
insights.so_what: Haircut timelines in operational-improvement theses; margin-expansion plans typically take roughly twice as long as modeled.
insights.quote: "Oh, let's take margins from 10% to 14%." You know, that's one click in my spreadsheet, but in reality in a business, that takes a lot more work to actually go do.

insights.claim: Usually only three to four things truly matter in a business or an investment; success comes from focusing time on those rather than the 100-page deck of other items.
insights.speaker: Tracy Britt Cool
insights.so_what: Underwriting and operating plans should be narrowed to the 3-4 key drivers that move the needle.

insights.claim: Berkshire had about $150 billion of cash when Tracy Britt Cool left and now has $300 billion plus, making it very hard to move the needle with check sizes, so the Berkshire model of 30-40 years ago (buying businesses like Benjamin Moore) is more interesting in the lower middle market.
insights.speaker: Tracy Britt Cool
insights.so_what: Berkshire's scale leaves the smaller 'Berkshire-like home' market under-served, creating room for long-hold mid-market acquirers.

insights.claim: Tracy Britt Cool believes the buyout era of buying at 7x and selling at 12x a few years later is probably over, so future returns must come from operating value creation.
insights.speaker: Tracy Britt Cool
insights.so_what: Favor PE managers with real operating capability over those relying on multiple expansion and leverage.
insights.quote: In the buyout world, the days of buying businesses for seven times and selling them for 12 a few years later was probably gone.

insights.claim: Very few buyout investors have actual operating experience (unlike venture), which is why Tracy Britt Cool left a chair role to become CEO of Pampered Chef: operating experience brings credibility and empathy with management teams and sellers.
insights.speaker: Tracy Britt Cool
insights.so_what: Operating track records are a differentiator in winning proprietary deals with founders and in driving earnings growth.

insights.claim: Cambrek enters new portfolio companies with 'listen and learn' and co-creates the strategy with management instead of imposing a 90-day plan, arguing co-ownership of the plan produces better outcomes.
insights.speaker: Tracy Britt Cool
insights.so_what: Post-acquisition approach that preserves management buy-in; a contrast to conventional PE 100-day plans.

insights.claim: Cambrek uses a 15+ year fund structure that self-selects long-term LPs and reassures founders worried about the 3-4 year private equity 'treadmill' of repeated flips.
insights.speaker: Tracy Britt Cool
insights.so_what: Long-duration vehicles are a sourcing advantage with family/founder sellers but don't fit LPs with short liquidity needs.

insights.claim: Cambrek owned JM Test for three years, roughly 4x'd its earnings, and returned its initial capital to investors via a recap while still owning 70%+ of a business compounding at 20%+ per year.
insights.speaker: Tracy Britt Cool
insights.so_what: Low-leverage compounders can deliver DPI through recaps without exiting, a model for evergreen/long-hold LP liquidity.

insights.claim: Cambrek puts little leverage on its businesses, so they generate substantial cash that can be returned to investors along the way instead of relying on exits.
insights.speaker: Tracy Britt Cool
insights.so_what: Low leverage trades lower IRR juice for cash yield and resilience; relevant to LPs comparing with levered buyout.

insights.claim: Tracy Britt Cool argues too many firms exit great businesses too soon because traditional fund structures and incentives force premature sales, and the bigger risk is selling too early rather than too late.
insights.speaker: Tracy Britt Cool
insights.so_what: Supports the continuation-vehicle/long-hold trend; the compounding of a known 20%+ grower beats redeploying into less-known risk.
insights.quote: our view is that too many firms exit businesses too soon.

insights.claim: Cambrek would sell a business if the market pays a silly price such as five years of future earnings today, if future earnings look riskier (e.g., AI disruption), or if another owner would be a better home.
insights.speaker: Tracy Britt Cool
insights.so_what: Defines explicit sell discipline for long-hold vehicles: valuation extremes, rising disruption risk, or better strategic owner.

insights.claim: Cambrek's edge is a mutually reinforcing 'three-legged stool' of long-term structure, the Cambrek CEO community and the Cambrek Business System, which compound together and are hard for competitors to replicate.
insights.speaker: Tracy Britt Cool
insights.so_what: Evaluate the moat of a PE firm by how sourcing, value-creation and capital structure reinforce each other, not by any single element.

themes.theme: CEO community as proprietary deal flow

insights.claim: Cambrek's CEO community has about 4,000 CEOs, owners and C-suite executives; all seven of its investments came through direct relationships and four of the seven came through the community.
insights.speaker: Tracy Britt Cool
insights.so_what: Content/education-led communities can be a scalable proprietary sourcing engine in the lower middle market.

insights.claim: The Cambrek community grew from a first 'Build with Cambrek' cohort of five CEOs to 127 CEOs by end of 2021, then 500, 1,000 and beyond, largely through referrals once the programs added value.
insights.speaker: Tracy Britt Cool
insights.so_what: Shows the referral flywheel timeline for community-led sourcing models.

insights.claim: Tracy Britt Cool believes more family and founder businesses will be transacted through relationships rather than auctions, because owners care about employees, legacy and future value creation, not only price.
insights.speaker: Tracy Britt Cool
insights.so_what: If true, auction-dependent buyers face adverse selection and relationship-led buyers can pay less competitive prices for quality assets.

insights.claim: About half of Cambrek's sellers are looking for a successor (a common trend among baby-boomer owners without an internal successor) and the rest are 'builders' who want a partner to scale.
insights.speaker: Tracy Britt Cool
insights.so_what: Baby-boomer succession gaps are a structural source of lower-middle-market deal supply.

insights.claim: In proprietary deals Cambrek asks owners what they think is a fair valuation and works through quality-of-earnings surprises jointly to reach win-win structures, which it argues an auction with ten bidders cannot achieve.
insights.speaker: Tracy Britt Cool
insights.so_what: Negotiated, non-auction processes allow flexible structuring (retained stakes, team protections) that can improve alignment and entry terms.

insights.claim: Cambrek reviews about 500 investments to do one or two and completes two to three deals a year; the most common reason a desired deal doesn't happen is the owner deciding not to sell rather than losing to another buyer.
insights.speaker: Tracy Britt Cool
insights.so_what: High selectivity; in relationship-led sourcing the competition is the owner's status quo, not rival bidders.

themes.theme: Underwriting quality: ROIC, moats and the five M's

insights.claim: Cambrek targets high-quality industrial services, manufacturing and some consumer businesses with $5-50 million of earnings, prioritizing business model and moat over sector.
insights.speaker: Tracy Britt Cool
insights.so_what: Defines the lower-middle-market niche where a Berkshire-style buyer competes.

insights.claim: Cambrek assesses quality first through return on invested capital and its trend over time, then qualitatively identifies the moat type (brand and channel, network effect, niche scale, route density) and whether it is strengthening or weakening.
insights.speaker: Tracy Britt Cool
insights.so_what: A reusable screen: ROIC trajectory plus moat-direction judgment.

insights.claim: Cambrek evaluates deals on five M's: moat, market, management, 'more potential' and margin of safety.
insights.speaker: Tracy Britt Cool
insights.so_what: Compact underwriting checklist for private-company investing.

insights.claim: Cambrek's early aftermarket marine boat-cover investment (patented track system, NPS in the 60s) at only about $2 million of EBITDA taught that its business system creates more value above $5 million of earnings.
insights.speaker: Tracy Britt Cool
insights.so_what: Value-add operating playbooks have a minimum scale; sub-$5M EBITDA deals can absorb disproportionate effort.

insights.claim: At the marine business Cambrek's second mistake was hiring a CEO with strong industry experience but poor cultural fit; replacing him with Steve Handel (ex-Red Ventures) course-corrected the dealer build-out and the business has doubled.
insights.speaker: Tracy Britt Cool
insights.so_what: Industry experience alone is insufficient in CEO hiring; cultural fit is a key risk in founder-transition deals.

insights.claim: JM Test, a 40-year-old family calibration-services business for industrial equipment measuring flow, pressure, temperature and electricity, has very sticky customers because calibration is a small cost relative to the cost of equipment failure, and it has 4x'd in 3+ years under Cambrek.
insights.speaker: Tracy Britt Cool
insights.so_what: Testing/inspection/calibration services are attractive moats (low price relative to failure cost) with roll-up potential among regional players.

insights.claim: Keep Supply, an industrial refrigeration business Cambrek recently partnered with, compounded at 70%+ for the last five years but had neglected customer segmentation and vendor relationships amid its fast growth.
insights.speaker: Tracy Britt Cool
insights.so_what: Fast-growing founder businesses often leave operational levers untouched that a partner can unlock.

insights.claim: Cambrek reports roughly 35% earnings CAGR across its companies, the vast majority organic rather than acquisition-driven.
insights.speaker: Tracy Britt Cool
insights.so_what: Organic-led value creation in the lower middle market as an alternative to buy-and-build multiple arbitrage.

insights.claim: Nearly every mid-size company has 15-20 mission-critical roles, and Cambrek starts each partnership by assessing talent in those roles.
insights.speaker: Tracy Britt Cool
insights.so_what: A practical diligence lens: map and grade the 15-20 critical roles in a target.

insights.claim: Cambrek's hiring process adapts GH Smart's 'Who' method (scorecard, proactive sourcing, structured selection with competency, culture and outcomes interviews, case study, assessments and backchannel references); GH Smart estimates 50% of hires are mistakes.
insights.speaker: Tracy Britt Cool
insights.so_what: Raising hire success from 50% toward 70-90% is a large value lever in people-driven mid-size firms.

insights.claim: At JM Test Cambrek identified turnaround time as the most critical KPI, built dashboards down to branch and individual level, tied incentives to it, and bonuses rose 3x in the first couple of years.
insights.speaker: Tracy Britt Cool
insights.so_what: KPI visibility plus aligned incentives can drive frontline productivity gains in branch-based service businesses.

insights.claim: Cambrek treats hiring and other non-CapEx spending as capital allocation decisions and often delays acquisitions at a new portfolio company until core operating muscle is built.
insights.speaker: Tracy Britt Cool
insights.so_what: Signals a core-first rather than roll-up-first value-creation sequencing.

insights.claim: Long hold periods justify building deep operating capability inside portfolio companies, which wouldn't make sense if a business were to be exited in four years.
insights.speaker: Tracy Britt Cool
insights.so_what: Holding period shapes the type of value creation; long-hold owners can invest in durable capabilities.

insights.claim: Cambrek has a team of 16 split into investing, community and business-system teams, with the business-system team (including talent, finance, tech and AI specialists) always the largest.
insights.speaker: Tracy Britt Cool
insights.so_what: Staffing mix reveals the firm's emphasis on operating value creation over deal volume.

themes.theme: AI and the premium on people

insights.claim: Tracy Britt Cool changed her mind on AI: while still disruptive for white-collar work, she now believes people, culture and relationships will be even more important and are underinvested in as a society.
insights.speaker: Tracy Britt Cool
insights.so_what: Businesses built on relationships and culture may be more AI-resilient; AI disruption risk is also a named sell trigger for Cambrek.
